items.headline: Orbital Matter to 3D‑print support structure for 5 kW solar array in 2028
items.title: Orbital Matter, EnduroSat Announce an In-Space Manufacturing Mission in 2028
items.scifi_hook: A startup will print solar‑panel frames in orbit, avoiding bulky folding designs.
items.eli5: They will use a space‑based 3D printer to build the frame that holds a solar array after launch.
items.why: It could simplify satellite design and lower launch mass.
items.text: Following off the success of its latest demo, in-space manufacturing startup Orbital Matter announced today that it would partner with EnduroSat for another mission in 2028, this time to deploy a 5 kW solar array with the help of Orbital Matter’s 3D printing capabilities. The demo aims to validate a new method to create large structures in orbit. Instead of folding bulky solar arrays into tight configurations to fit into launch vehicles, the companies plan to 3D print support structures in space to facilitate large solar-array deployments. “Basically, [folding] means that you need to design and develop all the space systems—all the spacecraft—mostly for the launch, and not for operations in orbit,” CEO Jakub Stojek told Payload. Copy and paste: The announcement comes shortly after Orbital Matter released results of its second demonstration mission, called Replicator 2, which proved the company’s ability to print structures in the vacuum of space for the first time. Replicator 2, launched on SpaceX’s Transporter-17 rideshare in July, using an EnduroSat bus. It carried four Orbital Matter printers, each equipped with liquid material which could be printed onto a spinning cylinder, and hardened using a UV light. As it prints, the hardened beam pushes out and holds a silicon solar blanket. items.headline: New model predicts internal solitary waves in the Sulu Sea
items.title: Scientists develop novel model to forecast internal solitary waves from multiple sources in the Sulu Sea
items.scifi_hook: Scientists can now predict hidden underwater waves that surf across the sea like invisible tsunamis.
items.eli5: A computer model uses physics equations and satellite data to forecast when and where internal waves will appear.
items.why: Improves maritime safety and ocean‑climate forecasting.
items.text: A research team led by Professor Li Xiaofeng from the Institute of Oceanology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (IOCAS) has developed a model to forecast internal solitary waves originating from multiple sources in the Sulu Sea. The model combines physical equations and satellite observations to predict wave arrival times and crest positions across this complex marine environment.
